A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Avat3r research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and supplementary material are readable and support comparison, including matching results moved between sections.

before.justification: v1 reports original avatar reconstruction and animation experiments, quantitative comparisons, component ablations, and supplementary studies of training subjects, input views and skip connections.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds quantitative comparisons, generalization demonstrations, identity-augmentation experiments and runtime measurements.

M1.justification: The Gaussian prediction architecture, DUSt3R/Sapiens components, expression cross-attention, skip connections and losses remain unchanged in Section 3. The single-view variant already appears in v1's supplement. Newly documented FLAME-code fine-tuning and activation caching do not establish a revision of the original algorithm.

E1.justification: Ava256 and NeRSemble remain the principal datasets; NeRSemble was already evaluated qualitatively in v1. v2 adds an internal dataset of 984 neutral identities for supplementary fine-tuning, extends single-image evaluation to NeRSemble, and includes additional phone captures with glasses, rotated inputs and a headscarf. These extend coverage within the existing head-avatar domain.

E2.justification: The four-image comparison expands from GPAvatar alone to GPAvatar, HeadNeRF and InvertAvatar. Supplementary single-image comparisons retain both GAGAvatar versions and add HeadNeRF and Portrait4D-v2 on NeRSemble. FlashAvatar is newly evaluated with a full monocular video. These are evaluated comparators, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: v2 introduces quantitative NeRSemble evaluation using 100 target images from six subjects, a white-background evaluation exception for HeadNeRF, additional fine-tuning conditions and a runtime protocol. It also tests the four-view-trained model with different inference view counts. The main JOD evaluation and its 100-frame video procedure disappear, although JOD remains in the retained skip-connection ablation. The original Ava256 split, evaluation resolution and base training schedule remain.

E4.justification: The original component, skip-connection and training-data/view-count ablations are retained. v2 adds extreme-expression interpolation, inference with three to six views using a four-view-trained model, challenging phone/accessory cases, a FlashAvatar viewpoint-failure comparison, and an experiment testing whether additional neutral identities improve identity preservation. Appendix C also adds an efficiency analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and scaling curves without uncertainty bands. Neither reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or statistical significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises Ava256 PSNR from 22.0 to 20.7 for Avat3r and from 20.3 to 19.4 for GPAvatar. Their LPIPS ordering reverses: 0.309 versus 0.304 becomes 0.33 versus 0.34. The reason for these revisions is unstated, so they do not establish a model improvement. v2 also adds NeRSemble, single-image, FlashAvatar, runtime and identity-augmentation results, while removing the main JOD scores. Existing ablation values remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation in Equations 1–18 is unchanged. Neither version contains additional theoretical propositions, proofs or derivations that change the comparison.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the central claims: an animatable large reconstruction model, few-image avatar creation through expression cross-attention, robustness to inconsistent inputs, and single-image applications using 3D GANs. The expanded experiments support these contributions without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 newly discusses identity drift and hypothesizes that additional neutral identities can improve identity generalization without extensive expression recordings. It attributes FlashAvatar's novel-view failures to overfitting and explains adaptability to different expression signals. The earlier temporal-smoothness interpretation accompanying JOD is removed. The stated limitations concerning GAN inversion, camera poses and lighting remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix E newly explains the expression-code sources and FLAME-code fine-tuning using GAGAvatar's Metrical Tracker for NeRSemble and in-the-wild driving. Appendix C documents activation caching and RTX3090 timing hardware. v2 also identifies published baseline implementations and the internal neutral-identity data source. Existing preprocessing, architecture hyperparameters, training budget and project website are retained.

R1.justification: Related work substantially expands through a new monocular-avatar reconstruction subsection, broader coverage of 3D GANs and inversion methods, and discussion of FaceLift and concurrent CAP4D and LAM. This develops the paper's positioning against video-based reconstruction and alternative single-image avatar approaches beyond v1's narrower treatment.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized introduction and related-work rewrites, adds a related-work subsection, moves the single-shot discussion into Appendix A.2, and reorganizes the supplement. The abstract, method exposition, training description, limitations and conclusion remain largely intact, so this is not a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The few-shot comparison becomes a full-width, multi-baseline display covering both datasets, and Table 1 gains dataset groups and comparator rows while losing JOD. New figures show interpolation, input flexibility, FlashAvatar failures, phone captures and identity augmentation; new tables report supplementary comparisons and runtimes. Existing figures are also relocated, including v1 Figure 3 becoming v2 Figure 18.

improvement.justification: v1's quantitative comparison relied on one baseline, while single-image and NeRSemble performance were illustrated primarily through examples. v2 substantially addresses this validation gap with multiple comparison methods, quantitative single-image and NeRSemble results, targeted generalization analyses, and measured creation/driving times. Expression-driving details also improve reproducibility. Removing the main JOD comparison weakens temporal-quality evidence, and unexplained changes to Ava256 scores limit traceability, but the broader and more informative validation provides a substantial net improvement.
